lesson.title: Writing It Right: The Homogeneity Setup
lesson.summary: Correct setup for a homogeneity test, identifying the groups, naming the response variable, and writing hypotheses in the homogeneity-specific template, is where most mistakes happen before any arithmetic starts.
lesson.body:
Getting the arithmetic of a homogeneity test right is the easy part. Getting the setup right, identifying the groups, naming the response variable, and writing hypotheses in the correct form, is where most mistakes happen.

Start by identifying the groups correctly. In a homogeneity setting, the groups are defined by how the data were collected, not by splitting one sample after the fact. In the study preference example from the previous chapter, School A, School B, and School C are three separate, independent random samples decided on in advance. A researcher who instead took one big random sample of students and then sorted them by school afterward would be setting up a test for independence instead, a distinction the next few chapters draw out in full. Next, identify the single categorical response variable measured the same way in every group, here, study preference with its three categories: alone, group, and tutor.

With the groups and variable identified, write the hypotheses using homogeneity's specific template:

H0: The distribution of the response variable is the same for group 1, group 2, and so on through group k.
Ha: The distribution of the response variable is not the same for at least one of the groups.

Applied to the schools example: H0 is that the distribution of study preference, alone, group, tutor, is the same for students at School A, School B, and School C. Ha is that the distribution of study preference is not the same for at least one of the three schools.

A few setup mistakes show up again and again. First, students sometimes write the hypotheses using independence language, saying school and study preference are independent, which mixes up the two tests. School here is not a second variable measured on one shared population, it is the design feature that produced three separate samples, so homogeneity's same distribution across groups phrasing is the right one, even though the arithmetic that follows is identical to an independence test. Second, dropping the context, writing something vague like the distributions are the same without naming both the variable and the groups, loses the specificity a proper conclusion needs. Third, unequal group sizes, 80, 90, and 70 students here, are not a problem to fix or flag. Homogeneity tests never require the groups to be the same size.

Setup also means revisiting the three conditions before trusting any resulting P-value: random, each group is its own independent random sample, independent, individuals independent of one another and each sample no more than 10% of its school's population if sampling without replacement, and large counts, verified in the previous chapter, every expected count at least 5. Only once the groups, the variable, the hypotheses, and the conditions are all correctly in place does it make sense to move on to computing the statistic.
